source.title: On the Opportunities and Challenges of Foundation Models for Geospatial Artificial Intelligence
source.authors: Geng-Chen Mai; Weiming Huang; Jin Sun; Suhang Song; Deepak R. Mishra; Ning-Hao Liu; Song Gao; Tian-Ming Liu; Gao Cong; Yingjie Hu; Chris Cundy; Zi-Yuan Li; Rui Zhu; Ni Lao

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It contains some formatting and OCR artifacts, but the relevant experimental tables and discussion are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Applies foundation models in new geospatial downstream-task settings and reports task scores across model sizes; it does not measure pretraining loss scaling itself.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling studies and states that LLM performance tended to scale with learnable parameters in toponym recognition. Its own relevant evidence is downstream-task performance across GPT sizes and prompting settings. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy, fit power laws, test extrapolation to much larger runs, or compare compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Supervised task baselines are not included as rows because they are not scale points for the claim.
record.test_reason: The study's own downstream scores across model sizes bear on V6 in new geospatial settings. It reports improving, nonmonotonic and reversed size trends, but fits no predictive scaling relation and measures no pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors find that some zero-shot or few-shot language models outperform supervised task-specific models on language-only geospatial tasks, while existing FMs generally lag on the tested multimodal tasks. They propose geospatial alignment for a multimodal GeoAI FM. They also report a tendency for toponym performance to improve with parameter count and explicitly observe that larger vision-language models need not perform better on remote sensing. They establish no pretraining-loss power law or compute-optimal allocation.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates downstream task metrics across existing models; it does not fit held-out pretraining-loss power laws or test compute-optimal training allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Task, model family/variant, and prompt setting (including zero-shot versus one-shot and raw versus conversational prompts) change the reported downstream results.
record.problems: For the tested scaling-related version, comparisons are downstream task scores rather than held-out pretraining loss. No fitted scaling curves, extrapolation checks, uncertainty estimates, or direct controls for model training/data differences are reported. Some evaluations use limited samples (Ju2016 API models: 544 examples) and the study reports different prompts/settings across tasks.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant score rows were left out under the 60-row limit. Task-specific baseline-model scores were not entered as scale results.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss and its power-law dependence on parameters, tokens or compute.
Prediction of larger-run loss from fits to smaller runs.
Fixed-compute optimisation of parameter and token counts and the stability of allocation exponents.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law functional forms in other modalities or training regimes; evaluating image models alone does not test this version.
Quantitative prediction from a fitted scale relation, prediction from pretraining loss, and prospective extrapolation to larger models.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices; prompt sensitivity alone does not test V7.

missing.what: Add vision-language size comparisons for street-view noise classification: OpenCLIP-L 427M, accuracy/F1 0.128/0.089; OpenCLIP-B 2.5B, 0.169/0.178; BLIP 3.9B, 0.452/0.405; OpenFlamingo 8.3B, 0.262/0.127. These are relevant downstream scale results omitted despite the record's completeness claim.

Add AID vision-language size comparisons under matched prompt settings. Original/updated accuracy: OpenCLIP-L 0.708/0.710; larger OpenCLIP-B 0.699/0.705; BLIP 0.500/0.520; OpenFlamingo 0.206. Corresponding F1 values are 0.688/0.698, 0.668/0.686, 0.473/0.494 and 0.154. Resolve the paper's inconsistent BLIP parameter counts: 3.9B in Table 6 versus 2.5B in Table 7.

Add POI precision and recall across sizes and shot settings because accuracy alone obscures class bias and changes the apparent ordering. For example, zero-shot GPT2 versus GPT-3 accuracy is 0.318 versus 0.144, while precision is 0.105 versus 0.448; one-shot ChatGPT Raw precision/recall is 0.524/0.245 despite accuracy 0.195.

Record forecasting MAE, MAPE and R2 where they change the size ordering. State-level MAPE worsens from 0.745 to 0.779 between GPT2-Medium and Large despite improving MSE; county-level MAE worsens from 94.3 to 99.8 and MAPE from 0.581 to 0.627 between GPT2-Large and XL.

record.verdict_notes: States use the preceding size point within each task and prompt condition unless otherwise specified. Reference points cannot establish a trend alone. Same-size training variants remain relevant context for V6 but do not isolate scaling. Table 1's metric arrows are inconsistent with the prose and are treated as errors. Reported ChatGPT parameter counts are unsubstantiated within the supplied study. No uncertainty estimates or fitted predictive curves establish statistical significance or quantitative predictability. The supplied manuscript is an arXiv v1 submission with placeholder publication metadata; it does not establish the record's peer-review claim.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fit is measured.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run losses.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens is studied.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The paper evaluates models on geospatial tasks, including image tasks, but does not test whether a power-law scaling form holds across modalities or training regimes.
The paper reports downstream task scores across model sizes, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss or formal, quantitative predictability from a fitted scaling relation.
It discusses prompt choices and task-specific limitations, but does not study scaling-law fitting choices or whether fitted exponents and compute-optimal allocations change.

relationships.condition: Few-shot Hu2014 toponym recognition, GPT2 size series through the paper's GPT-3 endpoint
relationships.reason: r01–r05 show accuracy increasing from 0.556 to 0.881; this supports a directional downstream size trend, without establishing quantitative predictability.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy increased from 0.556 to 0.881 across model sizes, without establishing quantitative predictability.

relationships.reason: r09–r13 show an overall GPT2 gain but a Medium-to-Large decline and a lower GPT-3 endpoint; the GPT-3 comparison also changes the evaluated sample.
relationships.display_finding: GPT2 improved overall but declined from Medium to Large, and GPT-3 scored lower while being evaluated on a different sample.

relationships.reason: r17–r21 show higher endpoint F-score but a GPT2-Large-to-XL decline from 0.518 to 0.481, so improvement is not consistent across sizes.
relationships.display_finding: F-score improved overall but fell from 0.518 for GPT2-Large to 0.481 for GPT2-XL.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot state-level dementia forecasting, MSE across GPT2 sizes and the GPT-3 endpoint
relationships.reason: r25–r29 show monotonically decreasing MSE from 44,635,055 to 587,263; low absolute GPT2 capability does not reverse this size trend.
relationships.display_finding: MSE decreased monotonically from 44,635,055 to 587,263 as model size increased.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot county-level dementia forecasting within the GPT2 family, MSE
relationships.reason: r33–r36 show every larger GPT2 worse than the 117M model: MSE 162,778–226,259 versus 77,529.
relationships.display_finding: Every larger GPT2 model had higher MSE, ranging from 162,778 to 226,259 versus 77,529 for the 117M model.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot county-level dementia forecasting, GPT2-XL to the paper's GPT-3 endpoint
relationships.reason: r36–r37 show MSE falling from 162,778 to 1,105, although the comparison changes training and model generation alongside size.
relationships.display_finding: MSE decreased from 162,778 to 1,105, although training and model generation also changed.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot UrbanPOI5K accuracy within the GPT2 family
relationships.reason: r41–r44 show accuracy falling at every size increase, from 0.318 to 0.001; the smallest model's majority-class bias qualifies the metric's interpretation.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy fell at every size increase from 0.318 to 0.001, although majority-class bias contributed to the smallest model's score.

relationships.reason: r48–r52 show nonmonotonic accuracy, including 0.317 to 0.057 within GPT2 and 0.324 to 0.176 from GPT2-XL to GPT-3.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy varied nonmonotonically, falling from 0.317 to 0.057 within GPT2 and from 0.324 for GPT2-XL to 0.176 for GPT-3.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot street-view noise classification, OpenCLIP size comparison
relationships.reason: Text-only evidence in Table 6, missing from the rows, shows 427M-to-2.5B OpenCLIP accuracy rising from 0.128 to 0.169 and F1 from 0.089 to 0.178.
relationships.display_finding: OpenCLIP accuracy increased from 0.128 to 0.169 and F1 from 0.089 to 0.178 as size increased from 427M to 2.5B.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot street-view noise classification across vision-language model families
relationships.reason: Text-only evidence in Table 6, missing from the rows, shows BLIP outperforming larger OpenFlamingo: accuracy 0.452 versus 0.262 and F1 0.405 versus 0.127.
relationships.display_finding: BLIP beat larger OpenFlamingo, with accuracy of 0.452 versus 0.262 and F1 of 0.405 versus 0.127.

relationships.condition: Zero-shot AID remote-sensing classification, both original and updated class-name prompts
relationships.reason: Text-only evidence in Table 7, missing from the rows, shows larger OpenCLIP below smaller OpenCLIP in both prompt settings, and the largest FM achieving only 0.206 accuracy.
relationships.display_finding: Larger OpenCLIP performed worse under both prompt variants, and the largest foundation model achieved only 0.206 accuracy.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GPT2 size series on Hu2014 toponym recognition
reader_labels.reason: The reported score rises across GPT2, GPT2-Medium, GPT2-Large and GPT2-XL; see r01–r04. This is evidence of a downstream size trend in this setting, not a tested predictive scaling law.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Other tested geospatial tasks and GPT variants
reader_labels.reason: The size/performance pattern is not consistent across tasks or model variants: newer large variants sometimes score below smaller GPT models, and POI results change with prompting; see r05–r08, r11–r16, r17–r24, r25–r54.
